title: Text-Based QR Phishing Bypasses Email Security and Image Scanners
content_md: Cybercriminals are increasingly using text-rendered QR codes to bypass email security tools designed to detect image-based phishing attacks, according to recent research highlighted by Kaspersky. QR phishing, also known as quishing, tricks users into scanning a code displayed in an email. The scan typically opens a phishing page on a smartphone, moving the victim away from a corporate browser, endpoint monitoring tools, and other desktop protections. The QR code also hides the destination URL until it is scanned. Traditional quishing attacks commonly use QR codes as attached or embedded images. Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) can inspect those images, decode the QR code, extract the URL, and check it against threat-intelligence feeds, reputation services, redirects, and known phishing domains. Email clients may also block remote images by default, preventing some QR codes from appearing at all. Text-Based QR Phishing Bypasses Instead of inserting a QR code as an image, attackers can build it directly inside an email using HTML markup, colored table cells, or text characters. The email client renders the black-and-white grid as a fully scannable QR code, even though no image attachment, embedded bitmap, or tag exists. This creates a detection gap. Image-focused scanners and OCR systems generally begin by locating an image object. A text-rendered QR shown in a laptop inbox and scanned from a phone.
